claims.claim: ADJUST-PE: in people 50 or over with a non-high/unlikely clinical probability, a D-dimer cut-off of age x 10 ug/L was used; of 331 people with a D-dimer between 500 ug/L and their age-adjusted cut-off who were left untreated, 1 had a clot event within 3 months.
claims.supporting_passage: To prospectively validate whether an age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff, defined as age × 10 in patients 50 years or older, is associated with an increased diagnostic yield of D-dimer in elderly patients with suspected PE. ... Patients with a D-dimer value between the conventional cutoff of 500 µg/L and their age-adjusted cutoff did not undergo CTPA and were left untreated and formally followed-up for a 3-month period. ... The 3-month failure rate in patients with a D-dimer level higher than 500 µg/L but below the age-adjusted cutoff was 1 of 331 patients (0.3% [95% CI, 0.1%-1.7%]).
claims.pico_timeframe: ED outpatients with suspected PE and non-high/unlikely clinical probability, age 50+; age x 10 ug/L versus 500 ug/L; adjudicated thromboembolic events at 3 months among untreated patients
claims.safe_wording: In a European study of 3346 emergency patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, people aged 50 or over whose clinical score was not high were not scanned if their D-dimer was below age x 10 (in ug/L). Of 331 people in that band between 500 and their age-based limit, 1 had a clot within 3 months.
claims.qualifications: Only after a clinical probability score (simplified revised Geneva or 2-level Wells). Management study with no randomised comparator. Assay and units matter (highly sensitive assay, ug/L; check the lab's units). The upper confidence limit for the failure rate is 1.7%, so 'safe' should not be read as 'zero risk'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Confidence interval 0.1-1.7% for failure rate. Other work (not opened) reports lower sensitivity with age-adjusted thresholds; the abstract-level evidence here is from one prospective study.

numbers.meaning: cut-off for age 50 or over (500 ug/L below 50)
3-month failure among patients between 500 ug/L and age-adjusted cut-off, untreated
prevalence of PE in the whole cohort

claims.claim: Among 673 people aged 75 or over with a non-high clinical probability, the share in whom PE could be excluded by D-dimer alone rose from 6.4% (43/673) with the 500 ug/L cut-off to 29.7% (200/673) with the age-adjusted cut-off, without any additional false-negative findings.
claims.supporting_passage: Among the 766 patients 75 years or older, of whom 673 had a nonhigh clinical probability, using the age-adjusted cutoff instead of the 500 µg/L cutoff increased the proportion of patients in whom PE could be excluded on the basis of D-dimer from 43 of 673 patients (6.4% [95% CI, 4.8%-8.5%) to 200 of 673 patients (29.7% [95% CI, 26.4%-33.3%), without any additional false-negative findings.
claims.pico_timeframe: Age 75+ with non-high clinical probability (673 of 766 aged 75+); 500 ug/L versus age-adjusted cut-off; PE excluded without imaging; false negatives over 3-month follow-up
claims.safe_wording: Among 673 people aged 75 or over whose clinical score was not high, a clot could be ruled out by blood test alone in about 6 in 100 with the fixed cut-off and about 30 in 100 with the age-adjusted cut-off (a rise of about 23 percentage points), and no extra missed clots were found in that group.
claims.qualifications: Subgroup (75+ with non-high probability, 673 people). 'No additional false negatives' means none found in the study; with about 200 people newly excluded, a small risk cannot be excluded (no confidence interval is given for this subgroup in the abstract). Differences are percentage points (29.7 minus 6.4 = 23.3). 'Ruled out' means no scan was needed after a negative score-plus-D-dimer pathway, not that clots are impossible.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Subgroup analysis; the abstract gives no subgroup-specific failure CI.

numbers.meaning: aged 75+, non-high probability, PE excluded with 500 ug/L cut-off
same group, PE excluded with age-adjusted cut-off
all patients aged 75+; 673 of them had non-high probability

claims.claim: NICE NG158 advises considering an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold for people over 50.
claims.supporting_passage: (Search-engine paraphrase, not verbatim) An NHS summary of the updated NICE guidance says it includes using an age-adjusted D-dimer when assessing people aged over 50.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state what NICE or UK guidance says. The post can say the rule was validated in ADJUST-PE and leave guidance out, or add a UK guidance statement only after the NG158 text is opened by a human.
claims.qualifications: Search extract only; NICE page cannot be opened; exact wording ('consider'), recommendation number and clinical-probability condition unconfirmed.

claims.claim: In 209,622 US veterans with CKD stages 3 to 5, older patients had higher death rates and lower treated end-stage kidney disease rates than younger patients at comparable eGFR; among those aged 85 or over the risk of death always exceeded the risk of ESRD.
claims.supporting_passage: However, among those with comparable levels of eGFR, older patients had higher rates of death and lower rates of ESRD than younger patients. ... Among those 85 years or older, the risk of death always exceeded the risk of ESRD in this cohort.
claims.pico_timeframe: US veterans, CKD stages 3-5 (eGFR below 60), baseline eGFR; all-cause death versus treated ESRD; mean follow-up 3.2 years
claims.safe_wording: In a 2007 study of about 210,000 US veterans with reduced kidney function (stages 3 to 5), people aged 85 or over were more likely to die over roughly three years than to start dialysis or transplant, at every level of kidney function studied.
claims.qualifications: All-cause death, not 'other causes'; 'treated ESRD' means dialysis or transplant, so untreated kidney failure is not counted; stages 3-5 combined, so not specific to stage 3 (the abstract does not give stage-3 figures); US veterans (sex mix not checked in the opened text, do not say 'mostly men' unless confirmed); observational; mean follow-up 3.2 years; 2007 data. It does not say kidney care is pointless: it says which outcome is likelier over a few years.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hallan 2012 (2 million people) found eGFR and albuminuria linked with mortality and ESRD at every age and argued that older adults should not be left out of CKD management. The authors of O'Hare conclude that age is a major effect modifier, 'challenging us to move beyond a uniform stage-based approach'.

numbers.meaning: share of the cohort aged 75 or over (cohort composition, not an outcome)
age group in which death risk always exceeded ESRD risk

claims.claim: Urine albumin gives risk information beyond eGFR at every age: higher albuminuria and lower eGFR were each linked with higher mortality and ESRD risk.
claims.supporting_passage: Mortality (112,325 deaths) and ESRD (8411 events) risks were higher at lower eGFR and higher albuminuria in every age category. ... Both low eGFR and high albuminuria were independently associated with mortality and ESRD regardless of age across a wide range of populations.
claims.pico_timeframe: 2,051,244 participants in 46 cohorts; eGFR and albuminuria versus all-cause mortality and ESRD; mean 5.8 years; adjusted
claims.safe_wording: In a pooled analysis of about 2 million people in 46 studies, both a lower kidney blood test (eGFR) and more albumin in the urine were each linked with a higher chance of dying and of kidney failure, in every age group, so the urine test adds information that the blood test alone does not.
claims.qualifications: Association, adjusted; does not by itself show what happens to an individual with stage 3 and normal albumin.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Albuminuria measured by dipstick in some cohorts.

claims.claim: A stage 3 CKD result with normal urine albumin carries a low risk of kidney failure in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: For example, even at age 75+ persons with eGFR 45–59 ml/min/1.73m and optimally low albuminuria had significantly increased mortality risk, though they had lower relative hazards and higher absolute risks than at younger ages.
claims.pico_timeframe: Age 75+, eGFR 45-59, lowest albuminuria category; mortality (not ESRD)
claims.safe_wording: Do not say a stable stage 3 result without albumin carries a low risk of kidney failure. Say instead that the urine albumin test adds information and that higher albumin goes with higher risk.
claims.qualifications: The opened full text gives no absolute ESRD risk for stage 3 with normal ACR. The passage found shows increased mortality risk even with low albuminuria at 75+, so 'reassuring' framing is not supported.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A stage-by-albumin absolute risk table (for example KDIGO heat map or kidney failure risk equation) was not opened.

claims.claim: CKD is defined by kidney damage or reduced GFR persisting for 3 months or more, so a single result needs repeating (the 'is it stable?' question).
claims.supporting_passage: CKD is defined as kidney damage or glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m(2) for 3 months or more, irrespective of cause. Kidney damage in many kidney diseases can be ascertained by the presence of albuminuria, defined as albumin-to-creatinine ratio >30 mg/g in two of three spot urine specimens.
claims.safe_wording: Chronic kidney disease is defined by kidney function that is reduced for at least 3 months, so asking whether the result has been repeated and has stayed the same is a fair question.
claims.qualifications: 2005 statement; current KDIGO 2024 and NICE NG203 wording not opened. The 'repeat before labelling' inference is mine from the definition; the statement does not say what a clinician must do after one test. 'Stage 3' means eGFR 30-59 in the standard staging (not stated in this abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; current guidelines not opened.

numbers.meaning: mL/min/1.73 m2, threshold in the definition

claims.claim: Some medicines are dosed or chosen according to kidney function, so a kidney result can change prescribing.
claims.supporting_passage: In clinical trials of dabigatran and rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF), drug eligibility and dosing were determined using the Cockcroft-Gault equation to estimate creatine clearance as a measure of renal function. ... Were the MDRD-derived eGFR to be used instead of Cockcroft-Gault in prescribing these new agents, many elderly patients with AF would either incorrectly become eligible for them or would receive too high a dose.
claims.pico_timeframe: 4120 people with AF in east London; anticoagulant eligibility and dose by kidney-function formula
claims.safe_wording: Some medicines, such as certain blood thinners for atrial fibrillation, are chosen or dosed by kidney function, so it is reasonable to ask whether any of your medicines depend on it.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is for one drug class; do not generalise to all medicines or to a particular dose threshold. The kidney measure used for dosing is often creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault), not the eGFR on the lab report (see C06-19). The claim that stage 3 label changes heart or blood pressure care was not sourced and should be left out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Another study (see C06-B2, PMID:38046038, not re-opened here) found no outcome difference by formula in very old people on DOACs.

numbers.meaning: of 1414 people aged 80+ with AF ineligible for dabigatran by Cockcroft-Gault who would have been judged eligible by MDRD (East London, 2013) - background only, probably not needed

claims.claim: Whether CKD should be defined by the same eGFR threshold at all ages is debated.
claims.supporting_passage: Supporters of the former approach have cited a dramatic rise in the prevalence of nephrosclerosis with age in kidney biopsies, even among healthy kidney donors, and suggested the concept of natural inevitable senescence of the kidneys suggesting age specific cutoffs for defining normal kidney function. ... In contrast, our meta-analysis documents that risk of mortality and ESRD is increased at approximately 60 ml/min/1.73m, the threshold used for defining CKD over the last 10 years, across all age groups.
claims.safe_wording: Doctors disagree about whether one kidney-function cut-off for 'kidney disease' suits every age; the post should take no side.
claims.qualifications: Authors of Hallan argue for a common definition; Delanaye 2019 (age-adapted definition) not opened, so cite no one for the opposing view beyond saying the debate exists.

claims.claim: KDIGO grades CKD risk by eGFR and albuminuria together; NICE NG203 recommends urine ACR alongside eGFR.
claims.safe_wording: Do not attribute this to KDIGO or NICE. Hallan 2012 supports that the two measures are used together to stage CKD ('recently ... suggested that the definition and staging of CKD ... should be determined by the combination of estimated GFR and albuminuria', background statement) but the guideline text was not opened.
claims.qualifications: KDIGO 2024 PubMed record has no abstract; NICE pages cannot be opened.

candidates.reason: ADJUST-PE abstract supports the rule, the condition (age 50 or over, after a clinical probability score), the failure rate (1/331, 95% CI 0.1-1.7%) and the 75+ subgroup figures (6.4% to 29.7%, no additional false negatives). Post must omit any statement about NICE/UK guidance (not opened), say 'in this study', stay with the subgroup wording, give the units (ug/L) and avoid implying zero risk.

O'Hare supports the death-versus-ESRD point but only as 'more likely to die than to receive dialysis or transplant', stages 3-5 combined, US veterans, 2007; 'other causes', 'stage 3 specific' and 'mostly men' are not supported by what was opened. 'Low risk with normal albumin' is not supported (Hallan shows increased mortality even with low albuminuria at 75+). Guideline (KDIGO/NICE) wording and heart/BP care claims not verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Lead with three questions: has the result been repeated over at least 3 months, what does the urine albumin test show, and does any medicine depend on kidney function. Then, as context, say: in a 2007 study of about 210,000 US veterans with reduced kidney function, people 85 or over were more likely to die than to start dialysis or transplant over about three years. Do not say the result is harmless or low risk, do not attribute to KDIGO or NICE, and note that doctors disagree on whether one threshold suits all ages.
